# Tim Smith — Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity (AToCC) & Attentional Synchrony

**Source work:** Smith (2012), "The Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity", *Projections: The Journal for Movies and the Mind* 6(1), 1–27 (+ Smith's eye-tracking studies and chapters)
**Evidence tag: 🟢**

**Sources opened (in the harvest):**
- "Exploring Inner Worlds" — a published dialogue between Tim J. Smith and Ian Christie
  (UAL Research Online PDF), in which Smith states his own findings in his own words.
- Smith's chapter "Audiovisual Correspondences in *Alexander Nevsky*: A Case Study in
  Viewer Attention", in *Cognitive Media Theory* (AFI Reader), Birkbeck e-print PDF —
  Smith's own academic text summarising AToCC and the gaze evidence.
- Theory paper (cited in both): Smith (2012), "The Attentional Theory of Cinematic
  Continuity", *Projections: The Journal for Movies and the Mind* 6(1), 1–27.

## (a) Core finding
Continuity editing works because a cut does the job of a natural shift of attention:
in real life you turn your eyes/head to a new part of the scene; in film the cut replaces
that movement. When a film is cut well, all viewers look at the same place at the same
time — **attentional synchrony** (Mital, Smith et al., 2011). Attention is pulled
involuntarily by motion onsets, faces and speech; a good cut (e.g. match-on-action,
cutting *just after* an action begins) rides those cues so the eye lands exactly where
the next shot needs it, and the cut itself goes unnoticed.

## (b) Evidence base
Laboratory eye-tracking: multiple viewers' gaze recorded frame-by-frame while watching
real film sequences (*There Will Be Blood*, Bond films, *Alexander Nevsky*), plus
behavioural probes. Gaze clustering during dynamic scenes has been **replicated by
numerous studies** (Smith's chapter: first observed by Stelmach and colleagues, "has
subsequently been replicated by numerous studies"). Computational work (Smith and
colleagues) showed points of high motion predict where viewers fixate and when synchrony
occurs. Smith is equally clear about the failure mode his data shows: in hyper-fast
"intensified continuity" (e.g. modern Bond/Bay action), viewers collapse to centre-frame
fixation, cannot recover between cuts, and over a long sequence this produces fatigue and
habituation — the arousal peak flattens and viewers get bored. Note: his "edit blindness"
work with John Henderson (2008) — viewers miss continuity errors because gaze is locked
on faces/action — is described in secondary summaries seen in search results (Putney
Debater blog; Bordwell's blog hosting Smith) but those pages were **not opened in full in
the harvest run**, so treat that specific label as reported-but-not-fully-verified here.

## (c) Tag: 🟢
Reason: attentional synchrony and motion-onset capture are measured, replicated
eye-tracking results, and AToCC is the peer-reviewed theory built directly on them.

## (d) Editing rules it converts into
- **R-SMI-1 (cut on motion):** IF you cut during an action, THEN cut just *after* the
  action has begun (match-on-action), so the motion onset carries the eye across the cut —
  never cut in the dead moment before movement starts. 🟢
- **R-SMI-2 (eye-trace landing):** IF the viewer's focus at the end of shot A is on a
  face/moving subject, THEN compose shot B so its subject of interest sits near the same
  screen area (or is the strongest motion/face cue) — the eye should not have to hunt
  after a cut. 🟢
- **R-SMI-3 (one magnet per shot):** IF a shot matters, THEN give it one dominant
  attentional magnet (face, onset of motion, spoken voice) and remove competing motion —
  synchrony collapses when two magnets fight. 🟢
- **R-SMI-4 (speed ceiling):** IF cutting rate gets so fast that a viewer cannot re-fixate
  between cuts, THEN slow down or hold a shot — beyond that point extra cuts buy fatigue
  and habituation, not excitement. 🟡 (Smith's measured observation + his stated
  interpretation of the Bond/Bay analyses.)
